hops.title: Say it: cold water grabs warmth fast
hops.text: "Water passes heat along about twenty-five times better than air!" Say it right before you chill the bowl, or when your child wonders why a cool pool feels chillier than a cool breeze. That is why cold water pulls warmth from your body so fast. So how does a seal stay warm while it swims?

sources.citation: OpenStax, University Physics Volume 2, 1.6 Mechanisms of Heat Transfer (thermal conductivity table)
Alaska Department of Fish and Game, Harbor Seal Body Condition
Washington State Parks, Cold Water Safety

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: A round harbor seal poking its head out of cold blue ocean water near small floating ice chunks.
image.caption: A seal's blubber slows the loss of its body heat as it swims in cold water.

hops.title: Compare it: an empty winter coat in a cool closet
hops.text: Take a puffy winter coat from a cool closet and let your child slip a hand into the empty sleeve. It feels chilly at first, then warms up from their own hand. A beluga whale wears a built-in coat like that: its blubber can be as much as 40 percent of its weight.

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: A parent and child seen from behind as the child reaches into the sleeve of a hanging winter coat.
image.caption: A coat holds in the warmth your body makes. A beluga's blubber keeps it warm the same way.

hops.title: Point at it: puffed-up birds on a chilly morning
hops.text: On a chilly walk together, stop a few steps back when you spot a bird sitting round like a fuzzy ball. Tell your child it did not grow bigger overnight. Birds fluff their feathers to trap air between them, which holds their own warmth close, much like a down coat.

sources.citation: The Raptor Center, University of Minnesota, What do birds do in Minnesota winter?

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: A small bird puffed up round with fluffed feathers, perched on a frosty tree branch.
image.caption: A chilly bird fluffs its feathers to trap air and keep its own warmth close.
